nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the fantastic tale and the bibliographer
literary_identity: Librarian, poet and story-writer; the Keeper of Printed Books at the British Museum and the author of The Twilight of the Gods.
biography: Born in Lichfield on 27 February 1835, the son of the assistant keeper of printed books at the British Museum; he joined the Museum staff in 1851 and rose to Keeper of Printed Books in 1890. His poems, his essays and above all The Twilight of the Gods and Other Tales (1888) made him a favourite of the connoisseurs. He died at Haslemere on 13 April 1906.
literary_profile: Richard Garnett wrote The Twilight of the Gods, the finest English collection of fantastic tales of the century and a founding text of the modern fantasy story: his stories of the gods, the philosophers and the impossible have been admired by every fantasy writer since, and his scholarship made him the central figure of the British Museum's golden age.
stylistic_characteristics: The ironic fantasy of the classical and the philosophical; the anecdote of the impossible; the dry, learned, understated narration; the epigram and the surprise ending; the frame of the historical or mythological occasion.
intellectual_concerns: Myth, ritual, and the primitive imagination; art versus life; the classical past and its gods; education and the book; death and the vanity of the world.
historical_significance: Richard Garnett wrote The Twilight of the Gods, the finest English collection of fantastic tales of the century: his stories of the gods and philosophers founded the modern literary fantasy and were admired by every writer of the genre since.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish-British; the City novel and the ghost story
literary_identity: Novelist; the first English novelist of the City of London and one of the finest Victorian ghost-story writers.
biography: Born Charlotte Eliza Lawson Cowan at Carrickfergus, County Antrim, on 30 September 1832; she moved to London, married the widowed novelist J. H. Riddell, and supported the family by her pen after his death. George Geith of Fen Court (1864), The Race for Wealth (1866), Austin Friars (1870) and the ghost stories Weird Stories (1882) followed. She died at Ashford, Kent, on 24 September 1906.
literary_profile: Charlotte Riddell was the first English novelist of the City of London and one of the finest Victorian ghost-story writers: George Geith of Fen Court opened the City to fiction, her financial novels gave the Victorian reader the world of the counting-house, and Weird Stories contains some of the best ghost stories in English.
stylistic_characteristics: The documentary detail of the counting-house and the ledger; the financial plot of speculation and ruin; the ghost story of the haunted house with its legal cause; the plain, businesslike prose; the sympathetic portrait of the working woman.
intellectual_concerns: Money, credit, speculation, and the joint-stock imagination; the metropolis, the crowd, and the imperial capital; the woman question, married disability, and the New Woman; the machinery of print: the serial, the magazine, and the book trade.
historical_significance: Charlotte Riddell was the first English novelist of the City of London and one of the finest Victorian ghost-story writers: George Geith of Fen Court opened the City to fiction, and Weird Stories contains some of the best ghost stories in the language.

literary_identity: Novelist; the author of Old Myddelton's Money, one of the most popular sensation novels of the 1870s.
biography: Born Mary Cecil Hay at Stoke-on-Trent in 1835; she wrote for the magazines and made her name with Old Myddelton's Money (1874), followed by Nora's Love Test (1876), Hidden Perils (1878) and A Wicked Girl (1880). She died in London on 24 April 1886.
literary_profile: Mary Cecil Hay wrote Old Myddelton's Money, one of the most popular sensation novels of the 1870s: its plot of the double life and the lost inheritance made it a circulating-library favourite and it shows the sensation formula at its most expert.

literary_identity: Novelist; the author of Comin' thro' the Rye, one of the great bestsellers of the 1870s.
biography: Born Ellen Buckingham Mathews at Misterton, Somerset, on 6 October 1853; she published Comin' thro' the Rye in 1875 and it sold in enormous numbers, followed by Cherry Ripe (1878), The Fashion of this World (1880) and many more. She died in London on 3 April 1920.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the religious problem novel and the suffrage heroine
literary_identity: Novelist; the author of Donovan and We Two, the most popular religious problem novels of the 1880s.
biography: Born Ada Ellen Bayly at Brighton on 25 March 1857; she published Donovan in 1882 and We Two in 1884, both bestsellers on the theme of religious doubt and unselfishness, followed by In the Golden Days (1885) and Doreen (1894). She was an active supporter of women's suffrage and died at Eastbourne on 8 February 1903.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the domestic novel for girls
literary_identity: Novelist; the most popular writer of the domestic novel for girls in the last quarter of the nineteenth century.
biography: Born Rosa Nouchette Carey at Bow, Middlesex, on 27 September 1840; she wrote Nellie's Memories (1868) and went on to publish some forty domestic novels, including Wee Wifie (1870), Heriot's Choice (1879) and Not Like Other Girls (1884). She died in London on 9 July 1909.

literary_identity: Novelist; the most prolific writer of the cathedral-town tale and the historical story for children.
biography: Born Emma Martin at Cromer, Norfolk, in 1830; she married James Marshall and, after the failure of his business, supported the family by writing. Her seventy-odd books include The Cathedral Cities of England, Under Salisbury Spire (1883), Under the Dome of St Paul's (1885) and The Master of the Guild (1891). She died at Clifton on 4 May 1899.

stylistic_characteristics: The cathedral and the close as setting; the historical episode folded into family history; the architecture and the music of the church; the plain, instructive, serial prose; the moral of the disciplined life.

biography: Born Evelyn Whitaker in London in 1844; she published Miss Toosey's Mission anonymously in 1878 and it sold in vast numbers, followed by Laddie (1880), The Awakening of Mary Fenwick (1882) and many more. Her identity was not made public until after her death in 1929.
